claims.text: What the image looks like Blunting of costophrenic angle, meniscus sign → pleural effusion (>200 mL on PA)
claims.quote: Blunting of costophrenic angle, meniscus sign Pleural effusion (>200 mL on PA)
claims.locator: Chest X-Ray (CXR), Air / Fluid in Pleural Space table

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) Diaphragm: R higher than L by ~1-2 cm; costophrenic angles should be sharp
claims.quote: D - Diaphragm: R higher than L by ~1-2 cm; sharp costophrenic angles; free air under diaphragm = perforation.
claims.locator: Chest X-Ray (CXR), Reading Approach (RIPE technical adequacy → ABCDE-FGHI)

claims.text: Examine the lateral upright chest radiograph when an effusion is suspected
claims.quote: The lateral upright chest radiograph should be examined when a pleural effusion is suspected.

claims.text: Upright film (Merck): 75 mL blunts the posterior costophrenic angle; blunting the lateral costophrenic angle usually requires about 175 mL but may take as much as 500 mL
claims.quote: In an upright radiograph, 75 mL of fluid blunts the posterior costophrenic angle. Blunting of the lateral costophrenic angle usually requires about 175 mL but may take as much as 500 mL.

claims.text: Lateral decubitus films (effusion side down) may detect small volumes more easily than upright films, particularly free-flowing effusions
claims.quote: Lateral decubitus radiographs (with the side of the effusion down) may be able to detect small fluid volumes more easily than standard upright radiographs, particularly with a free-flowing effusion.

claims.text: Larger effusions opacify portions of the hemithorax and may cause mediastinal shift; effusions > 4 L may cause complete opacification of the hemithorax and mediastinal shift to the contralateral side
claims.quote: Larger pleural effusions opacify portions of the hemithorax and may cause mediastinal shift; effusions > 4 L may cause complete opacification of the hemithorax and mediastinal shift to the contralateral side.

claims.text: Loculated effusions (trapped by pleural adhesions or within fissures) can be confused with a solid mass (pseudotumor), particularly in the horizontal or oblique fissure; lateral decubitus films, chest CT or ultrasound are more sensitive and should be done if it is unclear whether a density is fluid or infiltrate, or loculated or free-flowing
claims.quote: Loculated effusions are collections of fluid trapped by pleural adhesions or within pulmonary fissures. Further imaging (lateral decubitus radiographs, chest CT, or ultrasound) should be performed if it is unclear whether a radiographic density represents fluid or parenchymal infiltrates or whether suspected fluid is loculated or free-flowing; these tests are more sensitive than upright radiographs and can detect small fluid volumes. Loculated effusions, particularly those in the horizontal or oblique fissure, can be confused with a solid pulmonary mass (pseudotumor).

claims.text: Causes Transudate: some combination of increased hydrostatic pressure and decreased plasma oncotic pressure
claims.quote: Transudative effusions are caused by some combination of increased hydrostatic pressure and decreased plasma oncotic pressure.

claims.text: Exudate: increased capillary permeability → leakage of protein, cells and other serum constituents
claims.quote: Exudative effusions result from increased capillary permeability, leading to leakage of protein, cells, and other serum constituents.

claims.text: Most common transudate causes: heart failure, cirrhosis with ascites, nephrotic syndrome
claims.quote: The most common causes of transudative effusions are heart failure, cirrhosis with ascites, and nephrotic syndrome.

claims.text: Most common exudate causes: pneumonia, cancer, pulmonary embolism, tuberculosis
claims.quote: The most common causes of exudative effusions are pneumonia, cancer, pulmonary embolism, and tuberculosis.

claims.text: Symptoms Many cause dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain or both; some are asymptomatic and found incidentally on exam or chest radiograph
claims.quote: Some pleural effusions are asymptomatic and are discovered incidentally during physical examination or on chest radiograph. Many effusions cause dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, or both.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: thoracentesis if symptomatic; Light's criteria for exudate
claims.quote: Thoracentesis if symptomatic; Light's criteria for exudate
claims.locator: Chest X-Ray (CXR), Air / Fluid in Pleural Space table

claims.text: Light's criteria (exudate if ≥ 1 of 3): fluid LDH ≥ 2/3 ULN for serum LDH; pleural fluid:serum total protein ratio ≥ 0.5; pleural fluid:serum LDH ratio ≥ 0.6
claims.quote: Light’s criteria (≥ 1 of the following 3): | | 98 | 77 | Fluid LDH* | ≥ 2/3 ULN for serum LDH | 66 | 100 | Pleural fluid:serum total protein ratio | ≥ 0.5 | 91 | 89 | Pleural fluid:serum LDH ratio | ≥ 0.6
claims.locator: Criteria for Identifying Exudative Pleural Effusions (table)

claims.text: Thoracentesis for almost all patients with pleural fluid ≥ 10 mm thick on CT, ultrasound or lateral decubitus film that is new or of uncertain cause; generally not needed in heart failure with symmetric effusions and no chest pain or fever, where diuresis can be tried unless effusions persist ≥ 3 days
claims.quote: Thoracentesis should be performed in almost all patients who have pleural fluid that is ≥ 10 mm in thickness on CT, ultrasound, or lateral decubitus radiograph and that is new or of uncertain etiology. In general, the only patients who do not require thoracentesis are those who have heart failure with symmetric pleural effusions and no chest pain or fever; in these patients, diuresis can be attempted and thoracentesis avoided unless effusions persist for ≥ 3 days.

claims.text: Use ultrasound guidance for thoracentesis in all cases
claims.quote: Thoracentesis should be performed using ultrasonographic guidance in all cases, to improve procedural success and reduce complications (1).

claims.text: Small (< 10 mm on decubitus film or ultrasound), asymptomatic effusions generally need no treatment, because many resorb when the underlying disorder is treated
claims.quote: Small (< 10 mm of fluid on lateral decubitus radiograph or ultrasound) and asymptomatic effusions generally do not require treatment because many effusions resorb spontaneously when the underlying disorder is treated, especially effusions due to uncomplicated pneumonias, pulmonary embolism, or surgery.

claims.text: Larger symptomatic effusions need thoracentesis, except recurrent effusions with a known cause; chronic or recurrent symptomatic effusions: pleurodesis or intermittent drainage with an indwelling catheter
claims.quote: Larger effusions that are symptomatic require thoracentesis, except for recurrent effusions with a known cause. Effusions that are chronic or recurrent and causing symptoms can be treated with pleurodesis or by intermittent drainage with an indwelling catheter.
